summary: This document updates the cryptographic algorithm requirements for the Password-Based Message Authentication Code in the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), which is specified in RFC 4211. It moves the recommended algorithms to ones considered stronger today, so certificate requests protected by a shared password stay secure.

eli5.summary: Old locks get weaker as burglars get smarter. This document says which newer, tougher locks to use when someone asks for a digital ID card using a shared password.

questions: what iteration count should crmf use
subtitle: Swaps the aging SHA-1, DES and Triple-DES defaults in password-protected certificate requests for SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC.

tldr.problem: RFC 4211 defines a password-based MAC for certificate requests, but the algorithms it requires (SHA-1, HMAC-SHA1, DES-MAC, Triple-DES-MAC) were appropriate in 2005 and are no longer the best choices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9045 edits specific paragraphs of RFC 4211: the one-way function becomes SHA-256, the MAC becomes HMAC-SHA256 with AES-GMAC as a SHOULD, the iteration count guidance rises, and PBMAC1 is explicitly allowed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9045 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4211, so implementations of the certificate request format get stronger required algorithms without changing the message format itself.

today: RFC 9045 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021. It updates RFC 4211, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates RFC 9045 itself.

sections.title: Why the Algorithms Needed Updating
sections.content:
RFC 9045 updates the cryptographic algorithm requirements for the Password-Based Message Authentication Code (MAC) in the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), which RFC 4211 specifies. CRMF is how a party asks a certification authority for an X.509 certificate, and it is defined using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1).

The algorithms in RFC 4211 were appropriate in 2005, but the RFC lists three problems with them. HMAC-SHA1 is not broken yet, but much stronger alternatives exist. DES-MAC provides 56 bits of security, which is no longer considered secure. Triple-DES-MAC provides 112 bits of security, which is now deprecated.

The document works as a patch. It gives OLD and NEW text for specific paragraphs of RFC 4211, so the rest of that specification stays as it was.
sections.eli5: A lock that was good years ago may be easy to pick today. This document is a list of which old locks to throw away and which stronger ones to buy.

sections.title: Proof of Possession and PBMAC1
sections.content:
Section 4.1 of RFC 4211 covers proof-of-possession (POP) processing. In that text, the algId field identifies the algorithm used to compute the MAC value. Before this update, all implementations had to support id-PasswordBasedMAC and nothing else was mentioned.

The new text keeps that requirement: all implementations MUST support id-PasswordBasedMAC as presented in Section 4.4 of RFC 4211. It adds that implementations MAY also support PBMAC1, which is presented in Section 7.1 of RFC 8018.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know the main way to prove you hold the password. Now there is also an optional second way that some people may choose to learn.

sections.title: The Required Algorithms
sections.content:
The password-based MAC relies on a one-way function to compute a symmetric key from the password, and on a MAC algorithm. RFC 9045 changes the requirement for each.

  • owf (the one-way function): all implementations MUST support SHA-256. RFC 4211 required SHA-1.
  • mac (the MAC function): all implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA256. All implementations SHOULD support AES-GMAC with a 128-bit key. RFC 4211 required HMAC-SHA1 and said implementations SHOULD support DES-MAC and Triple-DES-MAC.

The ASN.1 identifier for HMAC-SHA256, id-hmacWithSHA256, is defined in RFC 4231. When it is used, the parameters SHOULD be present, and when present they MUST be of type NULL. The identifier for AES-GMAC with a 128-bit key, id-aes128-GMAC, is defined in RFC 9044.
sections.eli5: The old rule said to use three old locks. The new rule says to always have one strong lock, and it is also a good idea to have a second strong one.

sections.title: Iteration Count and GMAC Parameters
sections.content:
The iterationCount says how many times the hash is applied while computing the key. The slowdown makes dictionary attacks against the password harder. The minimum stays at 100, but the new text says it SHOULD be as large as server performance will allow, typically at least 10,000. A smaller count can be used when automated generation produces shared secrets with high entropy.

The password used to compute this MAC SHOULD NOT be used for any other purpose.

When AES-GMAC is used, the parameters MUST be present and MUST contain a GMACParameters structure with a nonce and a length.

  • The nonce is the GMAC initialization vector. It may have any number of bits between 8 and (2^64)-1 but MUST be a multiple of 8 bits, and it MUST be unique within the scope of any GMAC key. A 12-octet nonce is RECOMMENDED because it can be processed more efficiently.
  • The length is the MAC size in octets. GMAC supports 12 to 16 octets, but for CRMF the maximum of 16 octets MUST be used.
sections.eli5: Mixing the password many times makes guessing it slow. The new advice is to mix it a lot more, and never to reuse that password somewhere else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of the password-based MAC depends on how many times the hash is applied and on the entropy of the shared password. Cheap hardware support for hash calculation reduces the value of a high iteration count, so the entropy of the password is crucial.

The RFC gives numbers to show why. In 2010, researchers showed that about half of the real-world passwords in a leaked corpus can be broken with less than 150 million trials, indicating a median entropy of only 27 bits. With an alphabet of 60 characters, a randomly chosen 10-character password offers 59 bits of entropy and 20 characters offers 118 bits. A one-time password also helps, assuming the protected transaction finishes before an attacker can learn the password with an offline attack.

Implementations must protect both the password and the MAC key, since compromise of either may let an attacker undermine authentication. The RFC also notes that cryptographic algorithms age, which is the reason for this update.
sections.eli5: A strong lock does not help if the key is something easy to guess like a pet's name. Long random passwords matter most.

cells: Minimum of 100; SHOULD be as large as performance allows, typically at least 10,000
